doc.title: Jason Palmer interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 2, 2025

chapter: Sideman career and finding a sound
title: Sweets Edison on originality and recognizable sound
summary: Rowe quotes Sweets Edison on being an originator rather than an imitator.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: You make me think of, you’re talking about finding your own sound, and when we started this interview project back thirty years ago I was speaking with the older generation and a lot of them would say, “well everybody sounds the same now.” You know the sax players sound like either Charlie Parker or John Coltrane, and Sweets Edison was going on about how in his day you could recognize someone in one note, and he said this, he said, “We used to say we’d rather be the world’s worst originator than the world’s greatest imitator.”
And as for Sweets, he’s a good example. He plays a couple of notes and you can usually tell him.
